Agents burn tokens, and Graphify Cloud cuts that spend by 80%. It adds always-on memory that governs your agents, keeps code quality high, and proves correctness through formal verification. There's a free 14-day trial.

Run /graphify in your AI coding assistant and it turns your project into a knowledge graph covering code, docs, PDFs, images, and videos. You query the graph instead of grepping through files.

A few details on how it works:

Mapping code costs nothing and runs entirely on your machine. Parsing uses a tree-sitter AST, so it's deterministic and involves no LLM. Docs, PDFs, images, and video do get a semantic pass, which uses your assistant's model or a configured API key.

Every edge comes with an explanation. Connections are tagged EXTRACTED when they're explicit in the source, or INFERRED when graphify resolved them, so you can tell what was read directly from what was deduced.

There's no vector index underneath. No embeddings, no vector store. It's a real graph you traverse: ask a question, trace the path between two things, or get one concept explained.

If you want it running all the time, Graphify Cloud keeps the graph live across your entire SDLC. It supports monorepos and cross-repo work, does formal verification, and gives code review a bird's-eye view of your SDLC. Connectors for Sentry, Jira, and more put incidents and tickets in the same graph as your code. You can start the 14-day trial at app.graphify.com.

Autoresearch

Autoresearch turns Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an engine that keeps improving a target on its own.

The approach comes from Karpathy's autoresearch: set a constraint, define a mechanical metric, and let the agent iterate autonomously. Because each run builds on the last, the gains compound over time.

You set the goal. The agent runs the loop. You check the results when you come back.

You don't need AGI for this. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that keeps running.

The core skill, bundled runtime, installation, and verification surface support Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse. Hook guardrails are available for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Fork-and-flush handles plateaus the way Cai et al. describe in arXiv:2610.07447. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas, which adds randomness. The other half each receive a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log, following Zhang et al. in arXiv:2610.07625. In Guided mode, R sets the split. When the orchestrator hits a plateau, it forks before giving up. Details are in guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee is a read-only inventory collector for package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints.

It answers a narrow supply-chain question: when an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines show a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped, and EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response often needs a different view, though: the messy local state spread across lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee converts that scattered on-disk state into structured NDJSON component records. Given an exposure catalog, it flags exact matches, so responders who already know what they are looking for can run fast, read-only exposure checks.

ACI: Open-Source Infrastructure for Unified MCP Servers and VibeOps

This repo is for the ACI.dev platform. If you want the Unified MCP server built with ACI.dev, see aci-mcp.

ACI.dev is an open-source tool-calling platform that connects 600+ tools to any agentic IDE or custom AI agent. It gives agents intent-aware access to tools with multi-tenant auth, granular permissions, and flexible tool discovery, exposed either as direct function calls or through a Unified Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server.

As an example, instead of writing separate OAuth flows and API clients for Google Calendar, Slack, and other services, you can use ACI.dev to manage authentication and give AI agents unified, secure function calls. You can access these capabilities through our Unified MCP server or through our lightweight Python SDK, which works with any LLM framework.

You can also add a single unified MCP server to your favourite agentic IDE to speed up vibe coding and automate devOps. Configure the MCP with Vercel, Supabase, Cloudflare, and other platforms, then let AI handle provisioning, deployment, database configs, and debugging. LeanCTX sits between AI tools and the information they read. It picks the context relevant to a task, applies supported access and content controls before delivering it, and records the context operations and delivery evidence it can observe. Your application, agent loop and model remain yours.

CLI Printing Press

Time and money are the two things you can't get back. For AI agents, that means speed and token spend. A well-designed CLI becomes muscle memory for an agent: it never has to dig through docs, take a wrong turn, or waste tokens. That's why we built the Printing Press, a tool for printing the best CLIs in the world for agents.

It reads the official API docs, studies every popular community CLI and MCP server, and searches the web for APIs nobody published (think Google Flights or Dominos). Then it applies the power-user playbook Peter Steinberger proved with discrawl and gogcli: local SQLite, compound commands, agent-native flags. SkillsBench is a benchmark that measures whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across a range of domains. It shows how much a model's ability to solve complex real-world tasks improves when it has specialized Skills available.

To test performance in conditions closer to production, where many Skills are installed at the same time, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In the original setup, each task comes with only the specialized Skill for that task. In our version, every task runs in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, with all other experimental conditions unchanged. This lets us see whether an agent can find the right Skills in a large installed pool, combine them, and arrange them into a workflow that completes the task.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, while token consumption fell by 29.6% and tool calls by 33.1%.

sem is a semantic version control tool that sits on top of Git. Using tree-sitter, it parses your code and treats every function, class, and method as an entity, then diffs entities rather than lines. The result is a message like "function blahh was modified" instead of "lines x-y changed."

Any Git repo works, and there is nothing to set up.

Queries that use the cloud are opt-in for each repo, and logging in never uploads a repo or sends a query on its own. The cloud consent flow covers the public/private repo states, the preview screen, a local audit log, and forget controls.

It is part of the Ataraxy Labs stack of agent-native infrastructure for software development, alongside weave (an entity-level git merge driver), inspect (semantic code review), and opensessions (a tmux sidebar for coding agents).

Semantic version control built on Git.
